name: Hosting and maintenance
description: Hosting, backups, SSL, updates, uptime and support.

cards.subject: Shared hosting
says: places many customers' sites on one server and shares its CPU, memory and disk
gives the customer a control panel but no root access
is the cheapest-to-run model and suffers when a neighbouring site uses too many resources
cards.use: have a small brochure site with modest traffic and no special server needs
not: gives each site its own guaranteed slice of CPU and memory

cards.subject: A virtual private server
says: is a virtual machine with its own operating system and root access on a shared physical host
lets the administrator install any software stack but makes them responsible for patching it
gives dedicated memory and CPU allocations inside a larger machine
cards.use: need root access and your own software stack without renting a whole machine
not: leaves server patching to the hosting provider by default

cards.subject: A dedicated server
says: reserves one whole physical machine for a single customer
removes noisy-neighbour effects because no other tenant shares the hardware
leaves a hardware fault as a single point of failure unless a second machine exists
cards.use: need all of a physical machine's resources for one workload or for compliance isolation
not: shares its CPU with other customers' virtual machines

cards.subject: Managed hosting
says: has the provider patch, monitor and back up the server on the customer's behalf
puts operating-system administration inside the hosting contract instead of on the customer
suits clients who have no in-house person to run a server
cards.use: have a client with no technical staff who still needs a patched, monitored server
not: leaves operating-system patching entirely to the customer

cards.subject: Cloud infrastructure hosting
says: rents virtual machines, storage and networks by usage from a large provider
lets capacity be added or removed in minutes through an API
still leaves operating-system patching and application security with the customer
cards.use: need capacity that can scale up and down with demand
not: patches the guest operating system on the customer's behalf

cards.subject: Platform as a service
says: runs the customer's code on a provider-managed runtime without the customer managing servers
takes care of the operating system and runtime patching
restricts the customer to the languages, versions and add-ons the platform offers
cards.use: want to deploy application code without administering any servers
not: gives the customer root access to the underlying machine

cards.subject: Static site hosting
says: serves pre-built HTML, CSS and JavaScript files without running server-side code per request
reduces the attack surface because there is no application server or database to compromise
usually pairs with a content delivery network for global speed
cards.use: have a site whose pages can be built ahead of time and served as plain files
not: executes PHP on every page request

cards.subject: Container hosting
says: runs the application as an image together with its dependencies, so the same artefact runs in test and production
makes rollback a matter of starting the previous image
adds an orchestration and image-patching responsibility of its own
cards.use: want the identical packaged artefact to run in staging and production
not: removes the need to patch software inside the image

cards.subject: Colocation
says: places the customer's own hardware in a provider's data centre
supplies power, cooling and network connectivity but not the machine
leaves hardware replacement and servicing with the customer
cards.use: already own servers and only need a data centre's power and connectivity
not: supplies the server hardware as part of the monthly fee

cards.subject: A full backup
says: copies every selected file and database regardless of earlier backups
restores on its own without needing any other backup set
takes the most time and storage of the standard backup types
cards.use: need a self-contained copy that restores without other files
not: copies only what changed since the previous backup

cards.subject: An incremental backup
says: copies only what changed since the previous backup of any kind
needs the last full backup plus every incremental after it to restore
is the fastest and smallest backup type to take
cards.use: need the smallest and quickest nightly backup
not: needs only the last full backup to restore

cards.subject: A differential backup
says: copies everything that changed since the last full backup
needs only the last full backup plus the latest differential to restore
grows larger each day until the next full backup
cards.use: want a restore that needs only two backup sets
not: copies only changes since the previous backup of any kind

cards.subject: The 3-2-1 rule
says: keeps three copies of the data on two different media with one copy off-site
protects against the loss of a single disk, machine or building
counts the live data as one of the three copies
cards.use: are asked how many copies and where a sound backup plan keeps them
not: keeps three copies in the same data centre

cards.subject: An off-site copy
says: sits in a different location or provider from the live server
survives the loss of the host's whole account or data centre
is the copy that still exists if the hosting account is suspended or compromised
cards.use: must survive the hosting account itself being lost
not: is stored on the same disk in a different folder

cards.subject: A recovery point objective
says: states how much recent data the business can afford to lose
sets how often backups must be taken
is measured as time between the last good copy and the failure
cards.use: must decide how often backups run for a client
not: states how long the restore may take

cards.subject: A recovery time objective
says: states how long the site may be down before restore must be complete
drives the choice between a quick snapshot restore and a slow rebuild
is measured from the moment of failure to service being back
cards.use: must decide how fast a restore has to finish
not: states how much recent data may be lost

cards.subject: A restore test
says: proves a backup can actually be restored into a working site
finds corrupt, partial or password-protected backups before an emergency
is the only evidence that a backup job is worth trusting
cards.use: hear that backups report success every night but have never been opened
not: is satisfied by the backup job's success message

cards.subject: A retention policy
says: sets how long each backup is kept before it is deleted
balances restore choices against storage cost
decides whether a problem discovered weeks later can still be undone
cards.use: must decide how many days or weeks of copies to hold
not: decides how often the backup job runs

cards.subject: An immutable backup
says: cannot be altered or deleted for a set period, even by an administrator
survives ransomware or an attacker who has stolen the backup credentials
uses write-once storage or object lock features
cards.use: worry that an attacker with admin access could delete the backups too
not: can be edited by anyone holding the backup credentials

cards.subject: A server snapshot
says: captures a disk image at a point in time on the same provider
lets a whole machine be reverted quickly before a risky change
is lost if the provider account or storage fails, so it does not replace an off-site backup
cards.use: want a fast way back before a risky change on one server
not: is stored in a separate provider by definition

cards.subject: A database dump
says: exports a database as a consistent set of statements or a file
must be taken in a way that avoids a half-written state
is copied alongside the site files because files alone do not hold the content
cards.use: need a portable, consistent copy of the database
not: is complete once the site's files are copied

cards.subject: A security patch
says: fixes a known vulnerability in software
should be applied promptly because attackers study published fixes
usually carries lower risk of breaking things than a major upgrade
cards.use: see an advisory for software that a client's site runs
not: adds new features without changing security

cards.subject: A minor update
says: delivers bug fixes and small improvements within the same major version
rarely breaks compatibility if the vendor follows semantic versioning
is safe to batch into the routine monthly maintenance visit
cards.use: have a routine fix release within the same major version
not: is expected to remove old features

cards.subject: A major upgrade
says: may remove or change features and break compatibility with plugins or custom code
should be tried on a staging copy first
needs a rollback plan and a planned window
cards.use: face a move to a new major version of the CMS or of PHP
not: can be applied blind to production because it is only a patch

cards.subject: A staging environment
says: is a copy of the live site used to test changes before release
should match production software versions closely to be a meaningful test
must not send real emails or take real payments
cards.use: must test an update without touching visitors
not: is the live site itself

cards.subject: A maintenance window
says: is an agreed time slot when planned changes may cause disruption
is announced to the client beforehand
is picked for the period of lowest traffic
cards.use: must schedule a change that might briefly interrupt the site
not: is a period when no monitoring runs

cards.subject: A rollback plan
says: states how to return to the previous working state if a change fails
relies on a backup or the previous release taken before the change
includes a decision point for when to give up and revert
cards.use: are about to change a production site and need a way back
not: is written after the change fails

cards.subject: Automatic updates
says: apply patches without an administrator pressing a button
reduce the window of exposure to known flaws
carry the risk that an untested update breaks the site unnoticed, so monitoring must follow them
cards.use: want security fixes applied without waiting for the next visit
not: remove any need to monitor the site afterwards

cards.subject: End-of-life software
says: no longer receives security fixes from its maker
leaves every newly found flaw permanently unpatched
should be on a planned upgrade path before it ends, not after
cards.use: find the site runs a language version the maker has stopped supporting
not: still receives security fixes if the host promises to be careful

cards.subject: A vulnerability advisory
says: names an affected product, the versions affected and the fixed version
may be tracked by a CVE identifier
is what a maintainer reads to decide how urgent a patch is
cards.use: need to decide how urgently a reported flaw must be fixed
not: is a vendor's marketing announcement

cards.subject: A lock file
says: pins the exact versions of dependencies the build used
makes two installs on different machines resolve the same versions
should be committed so a deploy reproduces the tested build
cards.use: need two installs to resolve identical dependency versions
not: lets every install pick the newest version of each dependency

cards.subject: An uptime check
says: requests a page at a regular interval from outside the server
alerts when the response fails or times out
sees the site as a visitor does, unlike a check running on the same machine
cards.use: need to know quickly that a site has gone down
not: measures how long a visitor's browser takes to render the page

cards.subject: A status code check
says: compares the HTTP response code with the expected value
catches a 500 or 503 error page that a plain ping would call healthy
treats a 200 response as success only if that is the expected page
cards.use: want an alert when the server answers but with an error page
not: only tests whether the server answers ping

cards.subject: A keyword check
says: searches the returned page for expected text
catches a page that returns 200 but shows an error message or a blank body
can detect a defaced page when the expected text has vanished
cards.use: worry that the page returns 200 yet shows an error or is defaced
not: only checks the status code

cards.subject: A synthetic transaction
says: scripts a journey such as submitting a form or adding to basket
finds failures in a flow that a simple page check cannot see
runs on a schedule as a robot visitor
cards.use: need to know the enquiry form still works end to end
not: only loads the home page

cards.subject: A heartbeat check
says: expects a scheduled job to ping a URL on schedule
alerts when the ping stops arriving
detects a cron job that silently stopped running
cards.use: need to detect a scheduled job that has silently stopped
not: probes the public home page from outside

cards.subject: An alert threshold
says: sets the value at which a metric triggers a notification
must balance catching real problems against false alarms
is often combined with a short delay or repeat count before alerting
cards.use: keep getting woken by one-off blips and need alerts to mean something
not: turns notifications off for a metric

cards.subject: An escalation path
says: names who is told next if the first person does not respond
includes times after which the alert moves up a level
prevents an alert from sitting unread overnight
cards.use: must decide who is contacted when the on-call person does not answer
not: is the rule for how often backups run

cards.subject: A public status page
says: tells customers the current state of a service and any incident
reduces repeat enquiries during an outage
should be hosted separately from the service it reports on
cards.use: want customers to see an outage without having to email
not: is hosted on the same server it reports on

cards.subject: Disk space monitoring
says: warns before storage fills
prevents the database and logs from failing when the disk reaches 100 percent
should alert early enough for someone to act
cards.use: see logs and backups growing on a small server disk
not: only measures network latency

cards.subject: Log monitoring
says: reads server and application logs for errors and unusual patterns
reveals repeated failed logins or unusual requests
gives evidence for an incident report after the event
cards.use: need evidence of what happened on the server before an outage
not: checks whether a page loads from outside

cards.subject: A TLS certificate
says: proves the site's identity to the browser
lets the browser and server encrypt traffic between them
is shown by the padlock and the https address
cards.use: need the https padlock on a site
not: hides the site from search engines

cards.subject: A certificate authority
says: is the trusted organisation that issues and signs certificates
is trusted because its root certificate ships with browsers and operating systems
checks that the requester controls the domain before issuing
cards.use: ask who vouches for a certificate in the browser's eyes
not: hosts the website's files

cards.subject: The ACME protocol
says: lets software request and renew certificates automatically
proves control of a domain through a file or a DNS record challenge
is the mechanism behind automatic free certificates
cards.use: want certificates to renew without anyone remembering to do it
not: is an old manual process of emailing a CSR

cards.subject: Certificate expiry
says: makes browsers show a full-page warning once the date passes
is the most common reason a secure site suddenly appears broken
should be monitored with an alert days before the date
cards.use: find a site showing a security warning for a lapsed certificate
not: has no effect on visitors

cards.subject: A wildcard certificate
says: covers every one-level subdomain of a domain with a single certificate
needs a DNS challenge to prove control when issued by an automatic authority
makes one leaked private key a bigger exposure than a single-name certificate
cards.use: need one certificate for many subdomains of the same domain
not: covers the bare domain and every level of nested subdomain

cards.subject: A certificate chain
says: links the site's certificate through intermediates to a trusted root
breaks in some clients when the intermediate certificate is missing from the server
must be served complete by the web server
cards.use: find that some devices reject a certificate that works in a desktop browser
not: consists of the site's certificate alone

cards.subject: HTTP Strict Transport Security
says: tells browsers to use https only for the domain for a stated time
stops downgrade attacks to plain http after the first visit
is risky to set for a long time before every sub-service is on https
cards.use: must stop browsers from ever using plain http for the domain
not: redirects visitors from www to the bare domain

cards.subject: Mixed content
says: is an https page that loads some resources over plain http
makes browsers block or warn about the insecure items
is typically fixed by updating hard-coded http links after a migration
cards.use: see the padlock turn into a warning right after moving a site to https
not: is caused by an expired certificate

cards.subject: Cloudflare Full (strict) mode
says: encrypts the hop between the proxy and the origin and validates the origin's certificate
is needed when tokens or personal data cross the proxy-to-origin link
requires a valid certificate on the origin server
cards.use: must make sure sensitive data is encrypted all the way to the origin
not: sends the proxy-to-origin traffic over plain http

cards.subject: Cloudflare Flexible mode
says: encrypts visitor-to-proxy traffic but sends proxy-to-origin traffic over plain http
can cause a redirect loop if the origin itself forces https without reading the forwarded protocol header
gives visitors the padlock while the last hop stays unencrypted
cards.use: have an origin with no certificate that sits behind a proxy
not: validates the origin's certificate

cards.subject: An A record
says: maps a name to an IPv4 address
is what makes a domain name lead to a server
is replaced when a site moves to a server with a different IPv4 address
cards.use: need a name to point at a server's IPv4 address
not: maps a name to another name

cards.subject: An AAAA record
says: maps a name to an IPv6 address
is the IPv6 counterpart of the A record
needs to be updated or removed on migration as well, or visitors on IPv6 reach the old host
cards.use: need a name to point at a server's IPv6 address
not: maps a name to an IPv4 address

cards.subject: A CNAME record
says: makes one name an alias of another name
follows the target's addresses as they change
cannot coexist with other records on the same name
cards.use: want www to follow whatever address the main name resolves to
not: maps a name directly to an IP address

cards.subject: An MX record
says: names the mail server that accepts email for the domain
carries a priority number so a lower value is tried first
is what must be preserved when a website moves host but the email stays
cards.use: need to say where email for the domain is delivered
not: names the server that hosts the website

cards.subject: A TXT record
says: holds free-form text for a name
carries SPF, DKIM and DMARC policy and domain-verification strings
is how many services ask you to prove control of a domain
cards.use: must add a verification string or a mail policy to a domain
not: names the mail server

cards.subject: An NS record
says: names the authoritative servers for a domain
is changed at the registrar to move DNS to a different provider
decides which provider's records the world sees
cards.use: must move the domain's DNS to a different provider
not: points the website name to an IP address

cards.subject: DNS TTL
says: states how many seconds a resolver may cache a record
is lowered ahead of a migration so the change takes effect quickly
is raised again after the change to cut lookups
cards.use: plan a server move and want visitors to see the change fast
not: states how long the domain is registered

cards.subject: DNS propagation
says: is the period during which resolvers around the world still serve the old record
depends on the old record's TTL
is why some people reach the new site while others still reach the old one
cards.use: find that colleagues see the new site while a client still sees the old
not: is a delay caused only by the new web server starting up

cards.subject: SPF
says: lists the servers allowed to send email for the domain
is published as a TXT record
lets receivers reject or flag mail from unlisted servers
cards.use: must say which servers may send mail for the domain
not: adds a cryptographic signature to each message

cards.subject: DKIM
says: adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing mail
publishes the public key in DNS for receivers to verify with
lets receivers detect that a message was altered in transit
cards.use: must prove outgoing messages were signed by the domain
not: lists the servers allowed to send mail

cards.subject: DMARC
says: tells receivers what to do when SPF and DKIM checks fail and aligned
can request reports about who sends mail as the domain
is introduced with a monitoring policy before a strict one is enforced
cards.use: want receivers to reject spoofed mail from your domain
not: signs each message with a private key

cards.subject: A PTR record
says: maps an IP address back to a name
is set by the owner of the IP address, usually the hosting provider
is checked by some receiving mail servers when judging a sender
cards.use: find that the mail server's address has no reverse name
not: maps a name to an IPv4 address

cards.subject: Least privilege
says: gives each account only the access its job needs
limits the damage when one account or key is compromised
is why an API key should be restricted to the one action it performs
cards.use: must decide how much access to give a new key or account
not: gives staff the same admin access to avoid delays

cards.subject: Two-factor authentication
says: asks for a second proof, such as a code, besides the password
stops a stolen password alone from logging in
should be turned on for hosting, registrar and CMS admin accounts
cards.use: worry that a leaked password would give attackers admin access
not: makes the password longer

cards.subject: A login lockout
says: blocks further attempts after repeated failures for a period
slows password guessing
should apply per source address or account so a single attacker cannot keep trying
cards.use: see a flood of failed logins against the admin page
not: asks for a second proof besides the password

cards.subject: A web application firewall
says: filters web requests for known attack patterns before the application sees them
can block common injection and scanning attempts
does not replace patching the application
cards.use: want known attack patterns blocked before they reach the site
not: replaces the need for updates

cards.subject: Security headers
says: are response headers that tell the browser which protective behaviours to apply
include content-type sniffing, framing and referrer rules
cost almost nothing to add but must be tested for broken pages
cards.use: want browsers to enforce protective rules for the site
not: encrypt the page content

cards.subject: A content security policy
says: limits which sources scripts, styles and images may load from
reduces the damage of an injected script
can break a page if a legitimate third-party source is not allowed
cards.use: want to restrict which origins a page may load scripts from
not: forces all links to use https

cards.subject: File permissions
says: decide which accounts can read, write or run each file
should leave only upload and data folders writable by the web server
are a common cause of both breakages and compromises when set to 777
cards.use: must decide which folders the web server may write to
not: are set to 777 for convenience on a production site

cards.subject: Keeping secrets out of the web root
says: stores credentials and keys outside folders that the web server can serve
stops a misconfiguration from exposing configuration files to the public
keeps secrets out of version control as well
cards.use: must store a database password or an API key for a site
not: places the configuration file in the public folder with a hard-to-guess name

cards.subject: Removing unused plugins
says: reduces the code that can contain vulnerabilities
avoids leaving an unmaintained component installed
is cheaper than patching something that is not needed
cards.use: find several deactivated plugins sitting on a CMS
not: is unnecessary as long as the plugin is deactivated

cards.subject: Blocking directory listing
says: stops the server from displaying a folder's contents when no index file exists
prevents visitors from browsing uploaded and backup files
is a server configuration option
cards.use: find that visitors can browse a folder's file list in the browser
not: hides the folder from search engines only

cards.subject: A downloadable database file
says: is a breach if a web request can fetch it
can contain personal data and password hashes
should be tested for with a request that must return forbidden or not found
cards.use: need to confirm that a data file inside the site folder cannot be fetched
not: is safe because the file name is hard to guess
like: Keeping secrets out of the web root

cards.subject: Containing a compromised site
says: takes the site offline or behind a maintenance page
stops further damage to visitors while the cause is found
is done before cleaning begins
cards.use: learn that a site is serving malicious content to visitors
not: starts by deleting files at random

cards.subject: Taking a forensic copy
says: preserves the compromised files and logs before cleaning
gives evidence for finding the entry point afterwards
means the clean-up does not destroy the trail
cards.use: must keep evidence of what the attacker did before changing anything
not: replaces the clean backup

cards.subject: Finding the entry point
says: identifies how the attacker got in, such as an old plugin or a stolen password
prevents the same hole from being used again after the clean-up
uses access logs, file change times and the list of installed components
cards.use: have cleaned a site and want to stop it being hacked again the same way
not: is skipped because cleaning is enough

cards.subject: Restoring from a known-clean backup
says: replaces compromised files with a copy taken before the infection
is more reliable than hunting through files for every change
only helps if the backup predates the compromise and the entry point is closed
cards.use: need to be sure no hidden files remain on a compromised site
not: is safe to run without closing the entry point

cards.subject: Rotating credentials
says: changes every password, key and token that might have been exposed
covers hosting, database, CMS, email, FTP and API keys
is required even after the files are clean because the attacker may hold the old ones
cards.use: have cleaned a hacked site and the attacker may have seen the passwords
not: is unnecessary once the malware is removed

cards.subject: Hunting for persistence
says: looks for backdoors, new admin users and scheduled tasks left by the attacker
explains why a site gets re-infected after a clean-up
checks places such as uploads folders, cron entries and user lists
cards.use: find the same malware coming back a day after it was removed
not: is finished when the visible defacement is gone

cards.subject: Requesting a blocklist review
says: asks a search engine or safe-browsing service to re-check a cleaned site
removes the browser warning for visitors once approved
should be done only after the site is truly clean
cards.use: find browsers still warning visitors after the site is cleaned
not: should be requested before cleaning to speed things up

cards.subject: Notifying the client about a data breach
says: tells the client promptly if personal data may have been exposed
lets the client meet its own legal duty to report to the regulator, normally within 72 hours of becoming aware under UK GDPR
gives plain facts and next steps without guessing
cards.use: discover that customer data on a client's site may have been taken
not: waits until the investigation is fully complete

cards.subject: A post-incident review
says: records what happened, the timeline and the root cause
turns the incident into concrete changes such as monitoring or patching
is blameless and aimed at preventing recurrence
cards.use: have just resolved an incident and want to stop it happening again
not: assigns blame to the person who made the mistake

cards.subject: Page caching
says: stores a finished HTML page so it need not be rebuilt for every visitor
cuts server work on content that rarely changes
must be purged when content changes
cards.use: have a content site whose pages are rebuilt by PHP on every visit
not: caches only images and style sheets in the visitor's browser

cards.subject: Browser caching
says: tells the visitor's browser how long it may reuse a file without asking again
is controlled by cache headers such as Cache-Control
speeds up repeat visits for images, scripts and styles
cards.use: want repeat visitors not to download static files again
not: stores the rendered page on the server

cards.subject: A content delivery network
says: serves copies of static files from locations near the visitor
reduces load on the origin server
can also absorb traffic spikes and some attacks
cards.use: have visitors in many countries and want files to come from a nearby location
not: makes the origin server faster to boot

cards.subject: Image optimisation
says: resizes and compresses images before serving them
is often the largest single saving on a page
uses modern formats and correct dimensions
cards.use: find that a page weighs several megabytes because of photos
not: lowers the number of database queries

cards.subject: Lazy loading
says: delays loading images below the fold until the visitor scrolls near them
cuts initial page weight
should not be applied to the main image at the top of the page
cards.use: want below-the-fold images not to slow the first view
not: compresses the image file

cards.subject: Text compression
says: shrinks HTML, CSS and JavaScript responses with gzip or Brotli
reduces transfer size without changing the content
gives little benefit on files that are already compressed, such as JPEG
cards.use: want text responses to be smaller on the wire
not: resizes JPEG photos

cards.subject: Database indexing
says: lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table
speeds filtered and sorted queries
costs extra storage and slows writes slightly
cards.use: see queries slowing as a table grows to many thousands of rows
not: caches the finished page

cards.subject: Opcode caching
says: keeps compiled PHP in memory between requests
avoids reparsing the scripts on every request
is a server-side setting rather than a site change
cards.use: want PHP not to recompile its scripts on every request
not: stores database results

cards.subject: Object caching
says: keeps results of expensive queries or computations in memory
reduces repeated database work on dynamic pages
needs an in-memory store and careful invalidation
cards.use: have a dynamic page that repeats the same costly query for every visitor
not: stores the compiled PHP

cards.subject: Core Web Vitals
says: measure loading, interactivity and visual stability as real visitors experience them
include largest contentful paint, interaction to next paint and cumulative layout shift
can influence search ranking as a signal
cards.use: need a standard set of user-experience measures for page speed
not: measure only the server's CPU load

cards.subject: Time to first byte
says: measures how long the server takes to start responding
points to slow hosting, uncached pages or heavy queries when high
is separate from how long the page takes to render
cards.use: want to tell a slow server from a slow page
not: measures how stable the layout is while loading

cards.subject: A care plan
says: is a recurring agreement to keep a site updated, backed up, monitored and supported
sets out what is included and what is not
turns ad hoc fixes into planned, predictable work
cards.use: want a client's site looked after every month rather than only when it breaks
not: is a one-off build project

cards.subject: A service level agreement
says: is a written commitment on measurable service levels
may state response times, uptime and what happens when they are missed
should only promise what the provider can evidence and meet
cards.use: must put a measurable commitment in writing
not: is a marketing slogan

cards.subject: Response time
says: is how long until the provider acknowledges and begins on a request
is a different promise from how long a fix takes
may differ by severity
cards.use: are asked how quickly someone will start looking at a report
not: is how long the fix takes to finish

cards.subject: Resolution time
says: is how long until the problem is actually fixed
is harder to promise than response time because causes vary
should usually be given as a target, not a guarantee, except for simple cases
cards.use: are asked how long it will take to fix a problem
not: is how long until the first reply

cards.subject: A severity level
says: classifies how serious a problem is for the client
decides which response target and who is woken
treats a whole site down as more urgent than a cosmetic glitch
cards.use: must decide whether to work on a problem tonight or on Monday
not: is decided by who complained loudest

cards.subject: Support hours
says: state when requests are staffed
must be clear about whether weekends and bank holidays are covered
set client expectations for when a reply can be expected
cards.use: need to tell a client when someone will be available
not: are the same as the monitoring hours by default

cards.subject: A scope exclusion
says: states work that the plan does not cover
stops disputes by naming extras such as redesigns or new features

cards.use: have a client ask for a new page under the monthly plan
not: is hidden in the footer to avoid confusing the client

cards.subject: An uptime percentage
says: states the share of time a site is available over a period
translates into a downtime allowance, so a higher number leaves a smaller allowance
should state how planned maintenance is counted
cards.use: are asked to promise a figure for availability
not: guarantees that the site will never go down

cards.subject: A service credit
says: is the remedy offered when a promised level is missed
is usually a reduction on a future invoice
is only meaningful when the measurement method is agreed
cards.use: need to define what happens if an uptime promise is missed
not: is a free upgrade given for any complaint

cards.subject: A change request
says: is a formal ask for work beyond the agreed scope

cards.use: have a client ask for a feature that is not in the plan
not: is silently done to keep the client happy

cards.subject: A runbook
says: gives step-by-step instructions for a known task or incident

cards.use: want any trained person to handle a recurring incident the same way
not: is a list of passwords

cards.subject: An escalation to a developer
says: moves a problem the support person cannot solve to a more senior engineer

cards.use: face a fault that first-line support cannot fix

cards.subject: An update log

cards.subject: An uptime report

should state the measurement method
gives the client an honest figure for the promise made
cards.use: must show a client how available the site was last month
not: shows only the number of page views

cards.subject: A backup verification record

cards.subject: A security scan summary

cards.subject: A traffic summary

cards.subject: A plain-language summary

cards.subject: A pre-migration audit

lets problems be fixed before launch

cards.subject: Lowering the TTL

qa.q: Which hosting model gives a customer root access on a virtual machine but leaves operating-system patching to the customer?
qa.right: A virtual private server
qa.why: A VPS gives root access; patching it is the customer's job unless the plan is managed.

qa.q: Why is a nightly backup job that reports success not enough on its own?
qa.right: Only a restore test proves the backup can be turned back into a working site
wrong: Backups cannot be restored on a different day
Nightly jobs never include the database
qa.why: A job can finish while the archive is empty, partial or unreadable.

qa.q: What does the padlock in the browser address bar show about a connection?
qa.right: Traffic between the browser and server is encrypted and the certificate matched the domain
wrong: The website has been checked for malware
The business behind the site is trustworthy
qa.why: TLS covers encryption and identity of the domain, not the safety of the site.

qa.q: Which DNS record type tells the world where to deliver email for a domain?
qa.right: MX
qa.why: MX names the mail servers and their priorities.

qa.q: A client's site shows a full-page security warning this morning and was fine last week. What is the most likely cause to check first?
qa.right: The TLS certificate has expired
wrong: The CSS file is too large
qa.why: Expiry is the most common cause of a sudden certificate warning.

qa.q: Which of these should be switched on for hosting and CMS admin accounts first because it blunts stolen passwords?
qa.right: Two-factor authentication
qa.why: A second factor stops a stolen password from being enough.

qa.q: A client wants to lose no more than an hour of orders if the server fails. Which figure is that?
qa.right: The recovery point objective
qa.why: RPO is how much data loss is tolerable, and it dictates backup frequency.

qa.q: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule describe?
qa.right: Three copies on two kinds of media with one copy off-site
wrong: Three servers in two data centres with one spare
Three daily, two weekly and one monthly backup
Three passwords, two people and one vault
qa.why: It is the standard minimum for surviving a disk, machine or site loss.

qa.q: A site is on shared hosting and slows at the same time each evening although its own traffic is flat. What is the likely cause?
qa.right: Another tenant on the same server is using the shared resources
wrong: The TLS certificate is too short
The DNS TTL is too high
qa.why: Noisy neighbours are the classic shared-hosting problem.

qa.q: A monitor pings the server and reports healthy, yet visitors see a 503 error page. What check would have caught it?
qa.right: An HTTP status code or keyword check on the page
qa.why: A ping only proves the machine answers; a status or keyword check tests the page.

qa.q: When should a security patch for a widely used plugin be applied compared with a routine minor update?
qa.right: Promptly, because attackers study published fixes
wrong: Only at the next quarterly review
Never until a major version exists
qa.why: Exposure begins as soon as the fix is published.

qa.q: Which header-only measure tells browsers to always use https for a domain for a stated period?
qa.right: HTTP Strict Transport Security
qa.why: HSTS sets the https-only period.

qa.q: A client with no technical staff wants someone else to patch and monitor the server. Which hosting model fits?
qa.right: Managed hosting
wrong: A dedicated server on an unmanaged plan
qa.why: Managed hosting puts administration into the contract.

qa.q: Which of these does a response time in a support agreement describe?
qa.right: How long until the provider acknowledges and starts on the request
wrong: How long until the problem is fixed
How long the site stays up in a year
qa.why: That is the difference between response and resolution time.

qa.q: You are planning a server move on Friday. The DNS TTL is 86400. What should you do first?
qa.right: Lower the TTL several days ahead, at least one old-TTL period before the cutover
wrong: Raise the TTL so records are cached longer
Change the nameservers and then lower the TTL
Delete the old A record before the move
qa.why: Resolvers hold the old value for the old TTL; lowering it early shortens the switch.

qa.q: A site moves host and the contact form emails stop arriving. The domain's email runs at a separate provider. What is the likely cause?
qa.right: The MX records were lost when the DNS zone was recreated
wrong: The site's A record points at the old IP
qa.why: Recreating a zone without copying MX, TXT and other records breaks mail.

qa.q: A backup uses a full backup on Sunday and an incremental every other night. A failure happens on Thursday. What is needed to restore?
qa.right: Sunday's full backup plus Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday's incrementals
qa.why: Each incremental depends on the previous ones back to the full.

qa.q: The same plan uses a differential on weekdays instead. What is needed to restore on Thursday?
qa.right: Sunday's full backup plus Wednesday's differential
qa.why: A differential holds all changes since the last full backup.

qa.q: A plugin update on the live site breaks the checkout page. What should the maintenance plan have had ready?
qa.right: A rollback plan relying on a backup or previous version taken before the change
wrong: A status page on the same server
qa.why: Changes to production need a defined way back.

qa.q: Which is the better place to test a major CMS upgrade first?
qa.right: A staging copy of the live site
wrong: The live site during a quiet hour
A fresh blank install with no content
qa.why: Staging tests the upgrade with the real content and plugins without risk to visitors.

qa.q: Why would a runbook help a part-time support person during a night-time incident?
qa.right: It gives step-by-step instructions for known incidents so they can act the same way as an expert
wrong: It lists every password for the client
It removes the need for monitoring
qa.why: Runbooks capture how to handle repeat incidents.

qa.q: A client pays for a monthly plan and asks you to add a new booking feature. What is the right response?
qa.right: Treat it as a change request: quote it and get approval before starting
wrong: Build it silently to keep the client happy
Add it and raise the monthly price afterwards
qa.why: Work beyond the scope needs a quote and approval.

qa.q: After moving to https, a page shows a warning although the certificate is valid. What is the likely cause?
qa.right: Mixed content from a hard-coded http image or script
wrong: The DNS TTL is too long
The site has too few backups
qa.why: Resources still loaded over http make browsers warn.

qa.q: A page returns 200 but shows an error message in the body. Which monitor would detect it?
qa.right: A keyword check for expected text
qa.why: A status code alone looks healthy.

qa.q: Which report line best belongs in a monthly maintenance report for a non-technical client?
qa.right: Updates applied, backup restore test result and outages, in plain language
wrong: Every line of the access log
qa.why: Reports translate technical work into effect for the client.

qa.q: Which statement about response and resolution times is the one a provider can safely promise?
qa.right: A response time target, because the start of work is within the provider's control
wrong: A fixed resolution time for every fault
A guarantee that no outage will occur
That every fix takes under an hour
qa.why: Resolution depends on causes the provider may not control.

qa.q: A migration has finished and DNS is switched. Why keep the old host running for a few days?
qa.right: Visitors whose resolvers still hold the old address reach it, and it is a fallback
wrong: It costs nothing to keep so it is always done
The certificate will not work otherwise
Email cannot be delivered without it
qa.why: Propagation is not instant, and a rollback needs a live old host.

qa.q: A hosting account is suspended after a dispute. The only backups were stored on the same account. What rule was broken?
qa.right: The off-site copy of the 3-2-1 rule
qa.why: A backup that shares fate with the host is not off-site.

qa.q: Ransomware encrypted a server and the attacker had the backup credentials. Which backup type would have survived?
qa.right: An immutable backup
wrong: An incremental backup on the same disk
A server snapshot on the same provider account
A database dump in the web root
qa.why: Immutable copies cannot be altered or deleted for the retention period.

qa.q: A site has been cleaned, then the same malware appears again the next day. What most likely was missed?
qa.right: A backdoor, new admin user or scheduled task left by the attacker
qa.why: Persistence mechanisms and the entry point must be removed.

qa.q: You have cleaned a hacked site. Which step must come before restoring service?
qa.right: Rotate every credential that the attacker may have seen and close the entry point
qa.why: Otherwise the attacker returns with the old keys.

qa.q: A client's customer data may have been taken from their site. What do you do first about the client?
qa.right: Tell them promptly with plain facts so they can meet their own reporting duty
wrong: Wait until the investigation is complete
Delete the logs to avoid confusion
qa.why: Under UK GDPR the controller normally has 72 hours from becoming aware.

qa.q: Which migration approach lets you test the real domain on the new server before DNS changes?
qa.right: Edit the hosts file on your own machine to point the domain at the new server
qa.why: A hosts file overrides resolution locally.

qa.q: A deployment behind a proxy loops forever between http and https. The proxy talks to the origin over plain http. What is the likely fix?
qa.right: Make the origin's redirect use the forwarded protocol header instead of its own https variable
qa.why: The origin sees http on the proxy hop and keeps redirecting.

qa.q: An alert fires at 03:00 and the on-call person does not respond. What should have happened?
qa.right: The escalation path moves it to the next named person after a stated time
wrong: The alert is silently dropped until morning
The client is told to call their own developer
qa.why: Escalation prevents unread alerts.

qa.q: A client asks for 100 percent uptime in writing. What is the sound response?
qa.right: Explain that no provider can guarantee it and offer a measurable figure with a defined method
wrong: Agree, because it is only a number
Refuse to work with the client
Promise it but exclude every outage
qa.why: Only promise what can be evidenced and met.

qa.q: A shared hosting server blocks your .htaccess rules. What is the first thing to check?
qa.right: Whether AllowOverride is enabled for the site's directory
wrong: Whether the backup retention is long
qa.why: Without AllowOverride, .htaccess rules are ignored.

qa.q: A site's slow pages have a high time to first byte but small page weight. Where should you look first?
qa.right: The server: caching, slow queries and hosting capacity
qa.why: TTFB measures the server's response, not front-end weight.

qa.q: A restore test succeeds but takes six hours. The client expects a restore within one hour. Which gap is this?
qa.right: The recovery time objective is not met
wrong: The recovery point objective is not met
The backup retention is too short
qa.why: The test shows the time to restore exceeds the target.

qa.q: You set a DMARC policy to reject on a domain whose newsletter provider is not in SPF or DKIM. What will happen?
qa.right: Legitimate newsletter mail will be rejected
wrong: Nothing, because DMARC is advisory only
All mail will be delivered with a warning
The MX records will be removed
qa.why: Enforcement should follow a monitoring period to discover legitimate senders.

qa.q: A wildcard certificate's private key is copied to four servers. What is the second-order effect?
qa.right: One leaked key now exposes every subdomain at once
qa.why: Wider coverage widens the blast radius of a leak.

qa.q: A hardening change adds a strict content security policy and the checkout stops working. What is the most likely cause?
qa.right: A legitimate third-party script source was not allowed by the policy
wrong: The DNS record for www was removed
The backup ran during the change
qa.why: A CSP blocks any source not listed.

qa.q: Automatic updates are enabled for a client site. What must accompany them?
qa.right: Monitoring that detects breakage soon after an update
qa.why: Untested updates can silently break the site.

qa.q: A staging site sends real customer emails during testing. What was missing?
qa.right: Controls that stop staging from sending live email or taking real payments
qa.why: Staging must be isolated from real side effects.

qa.q: What does deploy-check.php do on the GGLink site?
qa.right: It only reports, changes nothing, and exits non-zero if anything would break the site
wrong: It creates the first admin account
qa.why: It is a report-only check and refuses to run over HTTP.

qa.q: A GGLink release has broken a page. Content is in the database. What does the deploy guide say to do?
qa.right: Restore the previous files and leave storage/ alone
wrong: Restore storage/gglink.sqlite over the live one
Delete storage/ so it is recreated
Run composer install on the server
qa.why: Enquiries keep arriving, so the database is not rolled back for a code fault.

qa.q: After a GGLink deploy, https://www.gglink.co.uk/storage/gglink.sqlite downloads a file. What does that mean?
qa.right: The .htaccess rules are not being honoured and must be fixed before going live
qa.why: It should return 403 or 404; a download is a possible data breach.

qa.q: Which line backs up the GGLink database before a release, per the deploy guide?
qa.right: cp storage/gglink.sqlite storage/backup-$(date +%F).sqlite
qa.why: A dated copy gives something to compare against or recover from.

qa.q: The GGLearn deploy script excludes certain paths from rsync. Which one protects the production database?
qa.right: data/*.db*
qa.why: Excluding the database files prevents a deploy from overwriting production data.

qa.q: In deploy/update-cloudflare-ips.sh, what is the purpose of the check on the number of matching lines before writing the file?
qa.code: [ "$(printf '%s\n' "$V4" | grep -cE '^[0-9.]+/[0-9]+$')" -ge 5 ] || { echo "unexpected IPv4 list, not writing" >&2; exit 1; }
qa.right: To avoid writing an empty or broken allow-list that would lock everyone out
qa.why: A bad fetch must never produce an empty allow-list.

qa.q: GGLearn's Apache vhost uses a plain Include for apache-cloudflare-only.conf. What happens if the file is missing?
qa.right: Apache refuses to load the configuration instead of serving the site to everyone
wrong: Apache serves the site to everyone silently
Apache skips the line and warns
qa.why: A plain Include fails loudly, unlike IncludeOptional.

qa.q: GGSocial's .env exists only on the server and a deploy uses rsync --delete without excluding it. What is the outcome?
qa.right: The .env is deleted, everyone is logged out and stored platform tokens cannot be decrypted
wrong: The .env is copied back from git
qa.why: Losing APP_SECRET invalidates sessions and encrypted tokens.

qa.q: On the GGLink server the live GGSocial :443 vhost is a regular file in sites-enabled that has drifted from sites-available. You edit the sites-available copy and run apachectl configtest. What happens?
qa.right: The test passes, Apache reloads, and nothing changes
qa.why: Edit the enabled copy, check with apachectl -S, back it up and then reload.

qa.q: The GGLearn database runs in WAL mode. Why does a plain copy of the .db file risk a bad backup?
qa.right: Recent writes may still be in the write-ahead log and be missed
wrong: The file is locked by the kernel
WAL mode deletes the database on copy
qa.why: deploy/seed-content.sh uses better-sqlite3's backup for a consistent snapshot.

qa.q: A drizzle-kit push would add a NOT NULL column to a table that has rows. How does GGLearn's deploy behave?
qa.right: It stops and fails the deploy because --force is deliberately not used
wrong: It runs a delete on the table and continues
It adds the column with random values
qa.why: Failing is preferable to deleting production rows.
